opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so my path into AI was a bit roundabout. I trained as a physicist, and what originally drew me to physics was this feeling that you were working on the most fundamental questions there were. But somewhere along the way I realized that a lot of the foundational work in physics had already been done, in a sense, decades ago. The big breakthroughs, quantum mechanics, relativity, happened in the early twentieth century, and much of what came after was refinement. As a young researcher, you want to be somewhere the important discoveries are still ahead of you, not behind you.

So I started asking myself: what's the field today that looks like physics did in the 1920s? Where are the foundational questions still open, but there's clearly something real and powerful underneath? And when I looked around, AI was the obvious answer. You had deep learning starting to work in ways nobody fully understood. There was AlphaGo, and the early results in language models, and it felt like we were watching the emergence of a new science in real time, with empirical results running way ahead of theory.

The other thing that convinced me was the leverage. If you make progress on intelligence itself, that progress compounds into every other field, including physics. So it wasn't really about abandoning science. It felt like betting on the science that would accelerate all the others. Once I saw it that way, it was hard to justify working on anything else.

r001.rationale: The response says physics once held the open foundational questions, while AI is the field that does so today, making foundational importance dependent on the historical era.

r002.rationale: It asks what field today looks like physics in the 1920s and identifies AI as an emerging science with major open questions.

r003.rationale: It mentions AlphaGo as part of the evidence that AI was advancing, but does not say it demonstrated powerful reasoning by a neural network.

fable-5.1.text:
I actually started out in theoretical physics. Growing up, the people I idolized were the physicists of the early twentieth century, the ones who were present for the big foundational discoveries, when the field was moving at an incredible pace and every few years somebody rewrote the picture of how the universe worked. That's what I wanted to be part of. So I did my PhD in theoretical physics, and what I slowly realized was that the field I had fallen in love with was, in some sense, no longer the field I was in. A lot of the deepest questions had either been answered or had become extremely difficult to make progress on, and the pace of fundamental discovery had slowed down enormously. You could spend a career on a problem and not know whether you'd ever see it resolved.

Around that same time, I started paying attention to what was happening in deep learning. This was around the AlphaGo era, and what struck me wasn't just the result, it was the texture of the field. It felt the way I imagined physics had felt a hundred years earlier. People were asking very fundamental questions about intelligence, about learning, about what it means for a system to generalize, and they were getting empirical answers quickly. Someone would have an idea, and within months you'd know whether it worked. That feedback loop is what makes a science alive.

And then there was the question of impact. If you really believe you can build systems that learn and reason in a general way, that's not a niche result. That's the kind of thing that touches every other science and every part of the economy. So for me the bet was pretty simple. There was a field where the most fundamental questions were still open, where progress was fast enough that one person could actually contribute to answering them, and where getting the answers right would matter enormously. Once I saw it that way, physics felt like the thing I loved for its history, and AI felt like the thing where the history was still being written. So I left and essentially retrained myself, and I've never regretted it.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts physics as the field of foundational discoveries in the early twentieth century with AI as the field where major questions are now being answered and history is still being written.

r002.rationale: It says deep learning felt like physics a hundred years earlier, with fundamental questions and rapid progress.

r003.rationale: It mentions the AlphaGo era as context, but does not say AlphaGo demonstrated powerful reasoning by a neural network.

astra-6.text:
For me, the compelling thing about AI was that intelligence sits upstream of almost every other scientific problem. In most fields, you’re using the intelligence you already have to understand something about the world. In AI, you’re trying to understand and build the thing that lets you solve those problems in the first place.

And that makes it a very unusual science to bet on. If you make progress on intelligence, that progress can potentially feed back into physics, biology, mathematics—really anything that requires reasoning and discovery.

But the other piece is that you can test your ideas. You can build a system, put it in an environment, and see whether it learns. So you have this enormous, fundamental question—what is intelligence?—paired with a very concrete experimental process. That combination is what made it so compelling to me.

r001.rationale: The response calls AI an unusual and foundational science, but does not say that which science is most foundational depends on the historical era.

r002.rationale: It does not compare AI’s scientific frontier with physics roughly a century earlier.

r003.rationale: It discusses building systems and testing learning, but does not mention AlphaGo or attribute inspiration to its demonstration of neural-network reasoning.

sol-6.1.text:
I came to AI through physics. What drew me to physics was the idea that you could take a complicated world and find a few principles that explain a lot of it. But over time, I became more interested in the thing doing the discovering. How do we learn those principles? How do we form abstractions, test ideas, and figure out what to try next?

That made intelligence feel like a particularly fundamental scientific problem. And it has this unusual property: if you make progress on it, you potentially improve our ability to make progress on every other scientific problem. You’re studying how discovery works while building something that can help you discover more. That combination made AI feel like the science to bet on.

r001.rationale: The response calls intelligence a fundamental scientific problem but does not say that the most foundational science depends on the historical era.

r002.rationale: It mentions physics as Laskin’s path into AI, but makes no comparison between AI’s frontier and physics roughly a century earlier.
